group_assessment.weighting: Pilot randomised, partially blinded trial of an enhanced (higher glucose infusion rate, higher lipid) versus standard parenteral nutrition protocol in the first week in 90 very low birth weight preterm infants, with neurodevelopmental follow-up (VEP at 4 months in 33, Bayley at 12 and 24 months in 46 and 29). The reported fact is no benefit and a slower P100 latency that disappears after adjusting for enteral intake, in a small and heavily attrited sample. A class-level data point on dextrose-rate intensity in neonates; not term encephalopathy, not a low-calorie regimen, not WWOX.

entries.proposition: Pilot randomised trial of enhanced versus standard parenteral nutrition in 90 infants under 32 weeks and 1500 g, with no formal power calculation and neurodevelopment as secondary outcomes.
entries.snippet: Given that this was a pilot/feasibility trial, we were unable to perform formal power analysis.

entries.proposition: The intervention group started a glucose infusion rate of about 5.5 mg/kg/min with protein 4 g/kg/day and advanced by about 1.5 mg/kg/min per day to 12-14 mg/kg/min; the control started at about 4 mg/kg/min and advanced by 1 mg/kg/min to the same maximum.
entries.snippet: GIR was advanced by ~1.5 mg/kg/min per day throughout the first week of life to a maximum of 12–14 mg/kg/min.

entries.proposition: The two arms differed in energy (parenteral kcal 65.2 versus 81.6) but parenteral protein was nearly the same (3.5 versus 3.6 g/kg/day); the contrast is mostly glucose and lipid.
Only 33, 46 and 29 of 90 infants had VEP, 12-month and 24-month follow-up respectively; the authors say follow-up was low because of the COVID-19 pandemic and that this jeopardises randomisation.
entries.snippet: While this is a randomized trial, the benefit of randomization is jeopardized when follow-up rates are low.

entries.proposition: Figure 1 flow diagram: 203 screened, 102 not included, 11 not eligible, 90 randomised, 87 with complete intervention data (45 control, 42 intervention); 4-month VEP 18 and 15, 12-month Bayley 23 and 23, 24-month Bayley 13 and 16.
entries.snippet: Visual attestation of the flow diagram (image nutrients-14-03890-g001): screened infants n = 203; subjects not included n = 102; not eligible n = 11; consented and randomized n = 90; died before 1 week of life 1, withdrawn due to metabolic disorder 1, incomplete data 1; infants with complete intervention data n = 87; control n = 45 and intervention n = 42; VEP 18 and 15; Bayley 12 months 23 and 23; Bayley 24 months 13 and 16.

experimental_context.system: preterm infants under 32 weeks, single NICU

entries.proposition: The intention-to-treat comparison found a longer P100 latency (slower processing) in the intervention group (145 versus 177 ms, p = 0.01).
entries.snippet: Univariate intention to treat the analysis of VEP data showed longer P100 latency in the intervention group, suggestive of slower speed of processing (control 145 vs. intervention 177 ms, p = 0.01).

entries.proposition: After adjusting for enteral calories (Model 2) the latency difference disappeared (estimate 22.81 ms, 95% CI -4.5 to 50.13, p 0.098).
entries.snippet: Multivariable analysis found a similarly longer P100 latency in the intervention group in adjusted Model 1 (for sex, gestational age, and age at VEP), but the difference disappeared in Model 2

entries.proposition: The Bayley scores at 12 and 24 months did not differ between arms.
entries.snippet: BSID outcomes were similar at 12 and 24 months CA (Table 3).

entries.proposition: Control infants in the follow-up groups had higher enteral intake (VEP group 31.4 versus 17.5 kcal/kg/day), i.e. enteral feeding differs between arms among those followed.
The text states a 10.13 ms faster processing per 10 kcal/kg/day of enteral energy, while the quoted effect estimate of -1.13 ms per kcal/kg/day would be 11.3 ms per 10 kcal/kg/day.
entries.snippet: there was a 10.13 ms faster speed of processing at 4-month VEP (effect estimate −1.13 (−2.011, −0.26) p = 0.013)

entries.proposition: Table 1 gives the same p value (0.475) for antibiotic days (2.2 versus 2.9) as for Apgar below 5; a duplicated value is likely.
The authors report no increase in hyperglycaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia or days of insulin with enhanced PN, and refer to a separate paper for it.
entries.snippet: In this trial, infants who had received enhanced PN did so without increased metabolic complications such as hyperglycemia, hypertriglyceridemia, hyperbilirubinemia, or increased days of insulin use when compared to the control group.

entries.proposition: The authors say the enhanced PN should be given with caution until larger randomised trials are completed; first-week enteral intake associated with better processing speed.
entries.snippet: Despite these differences in the follow-up groups, our findings suggest enhanced parenteral nutrition should be given with caution until larger randomized trials have been completed.
